title: Systems of linear equations
syllabus: Systems of linear equations and solutions
summary: The system Ax=b is consistent exactly when rank(A) equals rank([A|b]). It then has one solution if that rank equals the number of unknowns, and infinitely many if the rank is smaller. A homogeneous system is always consistent.
intuition:
A linear system asks for the columns of $A$ to combine to the right-hand side $b$. Writing $Ax=b$ with $A$ of shape $m\times n$, there are $m$ equations in $n$ unknowns. Consistency is not a question about $m$ versus $n$. A square system can have no solution, and a short wide system can have exactly one. The rank test sees the difference.

Form the augmented matrix $[A\mid b]$ by attaching $b$ as an extra column. The system has at least one solution if and only if $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$. Row operations that produce a row of zeros on the left and a nonzero number on the right are exactly the case where the augmented rank jumped. If the ranks agree, every equation is already implied by the others, and $b$ lies in the column space.

How many solutions is a second comparison, this time with $n$. If the common rank equals $n$, every variable is pinned down and the solution is unique. If the system is consistent and the common rank is strictly less than $n$, at least one variable is free and there are infinitely many solutions over $\mathbb{R}$. A homogeneous system $Ax=0$ always passes the rank test, because the extra column is zero and does not raise the rank. It always has the trivial solution $x=0$, and it has further solutions exactly when the rank is less than $n$.

definitions.body: The system $Ax=b$ is consistent when at least one vector $x$ satisfies it. This happens if and only if $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$.
Suppose $A$ is $m\times n$ and the system is consistent. The solution is unique when that common rank equals $n$. There are infinitely many solutions when the common rank is strictly less than $n$.
The system $Ax=0$ is homogeneous. It is always consistent. The solution set is the null space, a subspace of dimension $n-\mathrm{rank}(A)$.

formulas.name: Consistency
formulas.note: Unique solution when that common rank equals $n$, the number of unknowns. Infinitely many when the system is consistent and the rank is strictly less than $n$.

formulas.name: Homogeneous count
formulas.note: The zero vector is always a solution. It is the only solution exactly when $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$.

properties: $Ax=b$ is consistent if and only if $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$.
A consistent system in $n$ unknowns has a unique solution if and only if that common rank equals $n$.
A consistent system with $\mathrm{rank}(A)<n$ has infinitely many solutions. One free variable already gives a line of solutions.
A homogeneous system $Ax=0$ is always consistent, because $\mathrm{rank}([A\mid 0])=\mathrm{rank}(A)$ and $x=0$ is a solution.
For a square coefficient matrix, uniqueness is equivalent to invertibility: full rank, nonzero determinant, and trivial null space are the same condition.

examples.title: Consistent, with one free variable
examples.prompt: Solve $\begin{cases}x+2y+z=1\\ 2x+4y+3z=3\\ 3x+6y+4z=4\end{cases}$ and read the solution set off the ranks.
steps: The augmented matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&1\\2&4&3&3\\3&6&4&4\end{pmatrix}$. Replace row $2$ by row $2-2\cdot$ row $1$ to get $(0,0,1\mid 1)$, and row $3$ by row $3-3\cdot$ row $1$ to get $(0,0,1\mid 1)$.

Subtract the new row $2$ from the new row $3$ and the last row becomes $(0,0,0\mid 0)$. Two nonzero rows remain, so $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])=2$. There are $n=3$ unknowns and $3-2=1$ free variable. The system is consistent and not unique.

Back-substitution: $z=1$, and $x+2y+z=1$ gives $x+2y=0$. With free parameter $t=y$, the solutions are $x=-2t$, $y=t$, $z=1$. The particular vector $(0,0,1)$ satisfies all three original equations, because $A(0,0,1)^\top=(1,3,4)^\top$.
examples.answer: The system is consistent, the common rank is $2<3$, and the solutions are $(x,y,z)=(-2t,\ t,\ 1)$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$.

examples.title: The same coefficient matrix with a different right-hand side
examples.prompt: Keep the coefficient matrix of the previous example and replace the right-hand side by $(1,3,5)^\top$. Decide consistency. Then state what $Ax=0$ contributes for this $A$.
steps: The same row operations on $(1,3,5)^\top$ produce right-hand entries $1$, $3-2\cdot 1=1$, and $5-3\cdot 1=2$. The last row, after subtracting the new second row, is $(0,0,0\mid 1)$.
A zero row on the left with a $1$ on the right means $\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])=3$ while $\mathrm{rank}(A)=2$. The ranks differ, so there is no solution.
The homogeneous system with this $A$ is consistent regardless. Its null space has dimension $3-2=1$. The earlier calculation shows that the relation among the rows does not obstruct $b=0$.
examples.answer: The system with right-hand side $(1,3,5)^\top$ is inconsistent. The homogeneous system is consistent and has a one-dimensional solution set.

traps: Deciding existence from the shape alone. More equations than unknowns does not imply inconsistency, and fewer equations than unknowns does not imply infinitely many solutions. Compare $\mathrm{rank}(A)$ with $\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$ and with $n$.
Calling a homogeneous system inconsistent because it is allowed to have more than one solution. $x=0$ is always a solution. Extra solutions are a separate question.

Reading 'unique' off $\mathrm{rank}(A)=m$, the number of equations. Uniqueness needs the rank to equal the number of unknowns. A $3\times 2$ matrix of rank $2$ can give a unique solution of two unknowns; a $3\times 4$ matrix of rank $3$ cannot.

Forgetting the free-variable count is $n-\mathrm{rank}$, not $m-\mathrm{rank}$. In the worked system, $m-\mathrm{rank}=3-2=1$ happens to agree with $n-\mathrm{rank}$, and the next matrix of a different shape will not be so kind.
python:
def mulv(A, x):
    return [sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))]

A = [[1, 2, 1], [2, 4, 3], [3, 6, 4]]
assert mulv(A, [0, 0, 1]) == [1, 3, 4]
assert mulv(A, [-2, 1, 1]) == [1, 3, 4]
# row dependence: row3 - row1 - row2 = 0, and 4-1-3 = 0, while 5-1-3 = 1
assert [A[2][j] - A[0][j] - A[1][j] for j in range(3)] == [0, 0, 0]
assert 4 - 1 - 3 == 0
assert 5 - 1 - 3 == 1
assert 3 - 2 == 1  # free variables
print(1)

questions.stem: The system $Ax=b$ is consistent if and only if
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. Attaching $b$ does not increase the rank exactly when $b$ is already in the column space, which is the condition for a solution. Squareness, a zero right-hand side, and full row rank are different conditions. A zero right-hand side is sufficient for consistency, not necessary.

questions.stem: A consistent linear system in $n$ unknowns has a unique solution if and only if the common rank of $A$ and $[A\mid b]$ equals
options: the number of equations, whether or not that equals $n$
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. Consistency gives $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$. That number equals the number of unknowns exactly when there is no free variable, so the solution is unique. Equality with the number of equations is a different comparison and does not by itself pin down $n$ variables.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: A homogeneous system $Ax=0$ is always consistent.
A consistent system with $\mathrm{rank}(A)<n$ has infinitely many solutions.
Consistency of $Ax=b$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{rank}(A)=\mathrm{rank}([A\mid b])$.
A homogeneous system always has a unique solution.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The zero vector solves $Ax=0$, so a homogeneous system is consistent, and the rank test agrees because the extra column is zero. A free variable in a consistent system can be any real number, which is infinitely many solutions. Uniqueness for the homogeneous system needs $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$, so D is false.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&4&3\\3&6&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\4\end{pmatrix}$. Note that row $3$ of $A$ equals row $1$ plus row $2$, and $4=1+3$. Which of the following are true?
options: The system has a unique solution.
The system has infinitely many solutions.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. The row relation of $A$ is matched by $b$, since $4-1-3=0$, so the augmented rank equals $\mathrm{rank}(A)$. Elimination leaves two nonzero rows, and the rows $(1,2,1)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are independent, so the rank is $2$. Then $2<3$, the system is consistent, and there is one free variable, hence infinitely many solutions and not a unique one.

questions.stem: For the consistent system in the previous question, the number of free variables is an integer. Enter that integer.
questions.solution: The answer is **1**. There are $n=3$ unknowns and $\mathrm{rank}(A)=2$, so the number of free variables is $n-\mathrm{rank}(A)=1$. One parametrization is $y=t$, $x=-2t$, $z=1$.
